medical.title: A forgotten organ sheds new light on the origins of the ovary
medical.summary: How do ovaries develop? Much remains unknown. By studying the "rete ovarii," a small anatomical structure that has long been overlooked, a team at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) has uncovered the dual origin of the cells that surround and protect oocytes. This discovery offers new insights into ovarian development and opens up new avenues for research into fertility and gynecological cancers.

medical.title: New evidence suggests heart cells transmit electrical signals through more than direct connections
medical.summary: Your heart may beat 3 billion times or more over a long lifetime. Across 75 years or longer, it carries on without a thought while you sleep, work and exercise.

medical.title: Brain immune cells could weaken motor memories by removing myelin, study suggests
medical.summary: When people and other mammals learn new movements, connections between some of their brain cells become stronger. Yet studies have shown that learning motor skills also prompts changes in myelin, an insulating material around nerve fibers produced by cells called oligodendrocytes.

medical.title: Form and diversity: How tumor architecture shapes colorectal cancer progression
medical.summary: Tumors are not uniform, as even cancer cells within one patient can display extremely divergent characteristics and behaviors. This diversity, known as tumor heterogeneity, reduces therapeutic efficacy because cells in different states may respond differently to therapeutic interventions.

medical.title: Stronger molecular grip optimizes anticancer drug release
medical.summary: Researchers from Osaka Metropolitan University have modified a naturally occurring protein so that it can hold on to an anticancer drug more tightly, potentially preventing the drug from being released before it reaches its intended destination.

medical.title: Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease
medical.summary: A combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin produced results comparable to antibiotics when used alongside standard treatment for severe gum disease, with benefits persisting long after supplementation ended. The surprising discovery could offer an alternative for some patients while reducing reliance on antibiotics.

medical.title: The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men
medical.summary: Men and women appear to be similarly capable of multitasking, but men are more than twice as likely to ignore conversation while juggling multiple activities. Researchers believe this unexpected difference may help explain why women are widely perceived as better multitaskers.

medical.title: 'It's scary': California battles West Nile virus surge
medical.summary: For two months, Mandi Budd has been unable to use her legs—she is paralyzed because of a mosquito bite that nearly took her life.

medical.title: The same gene that helps define neuron identity may also balance developing brain circuits
medical.summary: A gene that helps set a neuron's identity also affects how many inputs it receives from other neurons. New research led by neuroscientists at King's College London finds that the molecules neurons use to wire together in the developing mouse brain depend on the role these neurons will play in the adult. The connections these neurons form also depend on how electrically active they are during development.

medical.title: Too much of this common nutrient could be accelerating blood vessel aging
medical.summary: Researchers have uncovered a kidney protein that may hold an important key to vascular aging and longevity. The protein helps prevent excess phosphate from accumulating in the blood and gradually turning flexible blood vessels rigid. In animal models, a deficiency accelerated blood vessel aging and significantly shortened lifespan, while reducing dietary phosphate helped lessen the damage.

medical.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
medical.summary: AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.

science.title: Protein redesign boosts DNA insertion activity and reveals how molecular machinery selects targets
science.summary: Genome engineering is exciting, given its vast potential to treat and even cure diseases, but it is still a largely uncharted biomedical innovation. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital recently uncovered the mechanisms involved in precisely integrating DNA into a target genomic location using CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs). By studying type I-F3 CAST, the researchers unveiled structural findings that explain how this CAST family achieves successful DNA integration at precise target sites and offer insights for future genomic engineering approaches. The results were published in Nature.

science.title: Scientists discover quasar formed within a mere 630 million years of the Big Bang, setting a record
science.summary: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.

science.title: Early Stone Age rock carvings in Scandinavia may have been signposts for hunting grounds
science.summary: Between roughly 9,000 and 4,000 B.C., artists in ancient Scandinavia painstakingly carved large, sometimes life-size images of elk, reindeer, bears and other creatures into rock faces teetering on the edge of fjords, rivers and lakes. But their meaning has long been debated.

science.title: Sensory deterrents aren't a 'one-size-fits-all' solution for sharks and rays
science.summary: A study on how select species of rays and sharks respond to sensory deterrents has reinforced why there isn't a one-size-fits-all solution to prevent fisheries bycatch.

science.title: Many buyers willing to pay more to know where their food comes from
science.summary: New research from Curtin University reveals many Australians are prepared to pay more for food when they know where it comes from and how animals are treated, despite ongoing cost-of-living pressures.

science.title: Mathematics fact fluency interventions for students with mathematics difficulties
science.summary: Associate professor Jonté Myers knows that developing fluency with mathematics facts is key to mathematics proficiency. However, many students struggle to develop these foundational skills.

science.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
science.summary: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.

science.title: 'King tide' waves batter California coast, soaking San Francisco
science.summary: Massive waves carried on king tides battered California's coast Wednesday, prompting evacuations and soaking San Francisco, but sparing feared mass disruptions to Thanksgiving holiday travel.

science.title: Some miniature Cas12m proteins can cut DNA after all
science.summary: An international research group led by graduate student Hayato Morinaga, Assistant Professor Satoshi N. Omura and Professor Osamu Nureki from the University of Tokyo has demonstrated for the first time that some Cas12m proteins do have an active state capable of cutting, or "cleaving," DNA. The team also clarified the structural differences between the active and inactive variations.

science.title: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
science.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-held, lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

science.title: Dragonflies feast on other insects during autumn migrations
science.summary: Dragonflies feast on a host of insects—and each other—during their autumn migrations, new research shows. Scientists studied dragonflies at the Pass of Bujaruelo—a 30-meter (98-foot) gap between two high peaks in the Pyrenees, through which millions of insects migrate every year.

science.title: Seeking Refuge on Resolution Island
science.summary: New Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.

science.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
science.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

science.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
science.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

science.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
science.summary: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

science.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
science.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

science.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
science.summary: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

science.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
science.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

science.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
science.summary: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.

science.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
science.summary: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling 16.1 billion miles from Earth to become the first spacecraft so distant that its signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe continues its historic journey through interstellar space, pushing the limits of human exploration despite dwindling power and technical challenges.

environment.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist

Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

environment.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets

Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

environment.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon

Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

environment.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
environment.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.

mix_items.title: Protein redesign boosts DNA insertion activity and reveals how molecular machinery selects targets
mix_items.summary: Genome engineering is exciting, given its vast potential to treat and even cure diseases, but it is still a largely uncharted biomedical innovation. By studying type I-F3 CAST, the researchers unveiled structural findings that explain how this CAST family achieves successful DNA integration at precise target sites and offer insights for future genomic engineering approaches. The results were published in Nature.

mix_items.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades

Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.

mix_items.title: The same gene that helps define neuron identity may also balance developing brain circuits
mix_items.summary: A gene that helps set a neuron's identity also affects how many inputs it receives from other neurons. New research led by neuroscientists at King's College London finds that the molecules neurons use to wire together in the developing mouse brain depend on the role these neurons will play in the adult. The connections these neurons form also depend on how electrically active they are during development.

mix_items.title: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
mix_items.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-held, lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

mix_items.title: Dragonflies feast on other insects during autumn migrations
mix_items.summary: Dragonflies feast on a host of insects—and each other—during their autumn migrations, new research shows. Scientists studied dragonflies at the Pass of Bujaruelo—a 30-meter (98-foot) gap between two high peaks in the Pyrenees, through which millions of insects migrate every year.

mix_items.title: Seeking Refuge on Resolution Island
mix_items.summary: New Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.

mix_items.title: Too much of this common nutrient could be accelerating blood vessel aging
mix_items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a kidney protein that may hold an important key to vascular aging and longevity. The protein helps prevent excess phosphate from accumulating in the blood and gradually turning flexible blood vessels rigid. In animal models, a deficiency accelerated blood vessel aging and significantly shortened lifespan, while reducing dietary phosphate helped lessen the damage.

mix_items.summary: Suncor, Canada’s second-largest oil company, wants to release treated wastewater from mining oil in Alberta’s tar sands into a drinking water source for the community of Fort Chipewyan. Investigative reporter Leana Hosea visited the community to learn more. She joins the Mongabay Newscast this week to detail what she found. “This story is not about […]

mix_items.summary: Tadeu de Oliveira, founder and leader of the Tiger Cats Conservation Initiative, a group of scientists committed to studying the smallest wildcats of South and Central America, wanted to be crystal clear: “It is rare to catch a tiger cat. mix_items.summary: The government of Ecuador has approved a new 10-year plan to promote economic activities that make use of the country’s biological resources, while also taking steps to conserve the ecosystems that they rely on. It aims to innovate agribusiness, ecotourism, and other industries in rural areas, without threatening the environment or Indigenous communities. The National […]

mix_items.summary: Despite promising developments, the 27 member states of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) have again failed to reach an agreement that protects the Southern Ocean. Mired by consensus decision-making and shrouded from public view by confidentiality rules, Antarctica’s governance systems are no longer fulfilling their mandate. This leaves room […]

mix_items.summary: The bare ridges of the Tunari mountain range rise high in Bolivia’s central Cochabamba department. Only the occasional stand of squat, shrubby trees and rust-red potato crops dot the slopes. It wasn’t always this way. The high-elevation landscape was once filled with native Kewiña (Polylepis sp.) trees, a slow-growing tree belonging to the rose family […]

mix_items.summary: ANATALYA, Türkiye — A year ago, a record number of Indigenous people attended the United Nations climate summit in Belém, Brazil. Although there as observers, without a seat at the negotiating table, they left with promises: recognition of their lands, a share of a new forest fund, and a just transition mechanism in the making. mix_items.summary: EDINBURGH — Ocean conservation efforts are being hindered by inadequate funding, as well as difficulties translating research into action, according to attendees of an international marine conservation congress in Scotland. Between Nov. 13 and 16, nearly 800 attendees from more than 65 countries convened in the Scottish capital, Edinburgh, for the eighth International Marine Conservation […]

mix_items.title: Indonesia fires test palm oil certification scheme as NGOs question RSPO accountability
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA — Environmental groups are questioning the effectiveness of a global organization that develops standards and certification for sustainable palm oil production after fires affected thousands of hectares in concessions belonging to its members in Indonesia — including areas certified under its sustainability scheme. The criticism came as the organization, the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm […]

mix_items.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
mix_items.summary: AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.

mix_items.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
mix_items.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

mix_items.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

mix_items.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
mix_items.summary: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

mix_items.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
mix_items.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

mix_items.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
mix_items.summary: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

mix_items.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
mix_items.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

mix_items.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
mix_items.summary: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.

mix_items.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
mix_items.summary: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling 16.1 billion miles from Earth to become the first spacecraft so distant that its signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe continues its historic journey through interstellar space, pushing the limits of human exploration despite dwindling power and technical challenges.

mix_items.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

mix_items.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
mix_items.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

mix_items.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

mix_items.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
mix_items.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.
